8788918.fragment: Who’s Ger Ger? Who’s dear Gerald

range.content: Who's Ger Ger? Who's dear Gerald

8788918.twitter_share_message: “Should read, “Who’s moth moth? Who’s dear Gerald? Dear Ger, that you? O dear, he is Gerald.” Thi…” —@Genius

children: Should read, “Who’s moth moth? Who’s dear Gerald? Dear Ger, that you? O dear, he is Gerald.” This points to the Italian philosopher Giordano Bruno who had an impact on Joyce. Bruno wrote extensively on the art of memory, a loosely organized group of mnemonic techniques and principles, and we see them mentioned in Virag Lipoti’s “testimony” at Bloom’s “trial” three times. But, much more importantly, are the hidden references to Bruno’s doctrine of the coincidence of contraries, by which he means: “Every power in nature or in spirit must evolve an opposite as the sole condition and means of its manifestation; and every opposite is, therefore, a tendency to reunion.” Joyce mentions this in an examination essay he took in Padua in which he adds that Bruno taught that these “contraries” create a power “without which man cannot fulfill himself.” So we see these opposites appearing in minor things such as the inverting of Virag’s name. Giordano Bruno was burned to death for his “heretical” views on February 17, 1600

8797874.twitter_share_message: “Matthew Arnold was an Oxford don who argued for a renewed religious faith and an adoption of cla…” —@Genius

children: Matthew Arnold was an Oxford don who argued for a renewed religious faith and an adoption of classical aesthetics and morals, particularly representative of mainstream Victorian intellectual concerns. A main theme Joyce borrows from his has to do with the effects of Hebraism and Hellenism. He writes: “At the bottom of both the Greek and the Hebrew notion is the desire, native in man, for reason and the will of God, the feeling after the universal order, — in a word, the love of God. But, while Hebraism seizes upon certain plain, capital intimations of the universal order, and rivets itself, one may say, with unequalled grandeur of earnestness and intensity on the study and observance of them, the bent of Hellenism is to follow, with flexible activity, the whole play of the universal order, to be apprehensive of missing any part of it, of sacrificing one part to another, to slip away from resting in this or that intimation of it, however capital.” The term “Hebraism” is used generally to infer the benefits and moral constraints of religion, while “Hellenism” refers to the “perfecting” effects of high culture. This is a significant and involved theme for Joyce, and to determine his intentions for its use is subject to discussion. Clearly drunkenness is not something Arnold would condone.

8799780.fragment: Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you

range.content: Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you

8799780.twitter_share_message: “The character “Bello”, vile and indecent himself has just carried out a barrage of indecencies t…” —@Genius

children: The character “Bello”, vile and indecent himself has just carried out a barrage of indecencies to humiliate Bloom. Joyce then has “him”, with fortified irony, rail against Bloom with “Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you;” it is Bloom being consigned to the lowest point of Hell – it is he being condemned for immorality by the vilest of wretches. The scene’s counterpoint in
The Odyssey

is in Book 10 wherein Odysseus begs Circe to let him leave to continue his journey home. She gives him the bad news that, before he can return home he must visit the Land of the Dead – Hell. When Odysseus points out to her that no one has ever visited there and returned, she gives him directions for the trip and tells him of the sacrifices he must make for a successful journey. In fact, Joyce has already placed Bloom at Hell’s depths. Are there to be hints as to how he might find a safe return?

children: Glad to see you adding links—but it’s better practice to add links
in this format
. The words to be clicked on inside [square brackets], the full link enclosed immediately afterwards within (ordinary parentheses).

You should still be careful about taking the exact same words from another source—it’s always best to put things into your own words. With basic factual info like this it’s not a big problem, but you should generally either place the words within quotation marks, or use your own phrasing and link to the source where you got the information from. Also: it would be better if you don’t simply identify an allusion and send users to the wikipdia page, but do a bit more research. In this case, there are several other online sources which discuss this specific moment. A bit of googling is all you need, as well as looking at the “References” and “Further Reading” secions on a wikipedia page.
A tidied-up version of this annotation (minus the picture), to
demonstrate by example, might look like this:
Photo Bits was a British magazine of softcore pornography which,
according to wikipedia
, was published between 9 July 1898 and 9 December 1914—available on the date Ulysses was set, then, but not on the day of its publication. Joyce certainly
knew the magazine
. See
this page
for a discussion on Joyce’s relationship to contemporary magazines.
I might edit this annotation myself, but it’d be great if you could propose an edit (not ncessarily doing exactly what I’ve done) on it yourself.
[You didn’t need to have included “It was mentioned in James Joyce’s Ulysses, because this is already an annotation on Ulysses. (Always
place asterisks
around the titles of books, in order to italicize them.) I hope this is all digestible, but do send me a message if you have any questions.=]
